body_markdown:
It’s with a quarter turn of opposite lock that my thoughts turn to retirement.


Specifically, how, in my golden years, I could drive this sleek silver pseudo-classic from the Sleepy Acres bridge club to a physio appointment and slide between the lines of the community rulebook.


The Porsche 550J, an official collaboration between Porsche and Britain’s Hedley Studios, could potentially fit the bill as a neighborhood electric vehicle (NEV), and it’s certainly an awful lot more entertaining than a golf kart.


You won’t be able to fit your clubs in, however, as this 80% scale model of the 1950s Porsche 550 Spyder has no trunk space. Barely room for two adults, in truth, but that was also true for the full-size car, where its tubular spaceframe chassis encroached significantly into the passenger space.


Hedley Studios has reduced this to maximize interior room, but not strictly to that 8/10ths scale. If you got a measuring tape out, you’d find various elements that are sized at about 60%, others pretty much at full-scale, but the net effect is a cohesive and confident reproduction, albeit in carbon fiber rather than sheet metal.


Simon Thompson


Simon Thompson


Simon Thompson


That confidence is most clearly demonstrated by having Porsche’s own museum-piece 550 Spyder on display alongside Hedley’s cars at the Porsche Experience Centre in Silverstone. Size aside, the most obvious differences between the two are inside, where the Hedley car has no shifter, and its gauges, while reflecting those of the OG 550, are repurposed for electric motor output and battery charge. Switches for the Drive/Neutral/Reverse, drive mode, and emergency cut-off are tastefully executed in aluminum, but a little incongruous, although the lighting controls are a delightful Bakelite-style period-look plastic. The same material can be specified for the thin-rimmed three-spoke steering wheel, or a wood-rimmed Nardi is also available. The hefty fly-off handbrake and pedals are also aluminum.


Simon Thompson


Although the doors look like they open, they don’t, so to get in I have to step over the side and drop down into the driver’s seat. The steering wheel has a quick-release to make access easier and add a little parked-up pizzazz.


First thing to note: the 550J is seriously low to the ground. Think go-kart, not golf cart. Yet there’s proper car engineering in the chassis. In total, there’s said to be more than 1300 engineered components, including Eibach springs and Bilstein dampers for the twin trailing-arm front suspension and swing-axle rear end. Brembo disc brakes (from a Ducati) provide the stopping power, and Continental tires take care of grip.


There’s a choice of two motor specs. As standard, the 48-volt powertrain sends 11 hp (8kW) to the rear wheels, fed by two 1.8 kWh lithium-ion battery packs. Choose the RS model, though, and you get 21 hp (16 kW) and four battery packs. The former provides a range of around 30 miles and a top speed of 40 mph; the latter raises the stakes to 50 miles and 50 mph, while also upgrading the brakes to drilled discs and sintered pads, and swapping the Bilsteins for adjustable items, while Alcantara replaces the standard-issue black leather trim.


Only 250 550Js are to be built in total, and each one is expected to be unique. Buyers have so far requested paint and trim to match existing cars in their collections, even down to period patina; others have asked to replicate[James Dean’s machine](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/the-haunting-story-of-james-deans-little-bastard/) . Fine Silver is the standard color, but the full complement of Porsche’s Paint-to-Sample hues is available, as well as bare carbon, and all manner of racing stripes and decals. Pricing starts at around $94,000 before taxes.


Simon Thompson


It’s the RS that I drive first on Porsche’s private test track next to the British Grand Prix circuit. While it does have painted curbs, the layout is more like an English country road, constantly twisting and turning, rising and falling.


Following an instructor in a Taycan, it’s pretty much flat-out everywhere, with the petite Porsche tipping into each corner confidently. Acceleration is plenty lively and braking suitably up to scratch, but the real fun begins when I give it a mid-bend lift of the throttle or trail-brake on turn-in. Now there’s a lovely moment of weight transfer where the 550J steers from the rear. In the RS there’s just enough power to hold the ensuing slide if I floor it, while even the less potent standard car will shimmy its rear when invited.


Simon Thompson


Founder Ben Hedley says the team wasn’t able to benchmark the 550J against the original but still wanted to make it playful. Hedley is a Caterham racer himself and has made sure that every one of the company’s scaled-down cars actually handles properly.


It’s with visible disappointment, then, that he admits only around 20 per cent of the more than 500 Bugattis, Bentleys, Aston Martins and Ferraris Hedley has built so far are actually driven regularly by their owners, with the rest being treated as collectible art pieces. Hedley says he’d love to see them race, or at least be driven in areas where the rules of the road allow (only the Bentley Blower Junior is actually homologated for general road use).


Around 40% of[Hedley’s cars](https://hedleystudios.com/) have been exported to the U.S. I do hope at least some owners are sending them through the streets of their “active adult” communities. It’s certainly what I’d do.


Simon Thompson
